---
title: "EMD via L1 distance between CDFs in 1D"

  html_document:

## Setup and notation

Let $k$ be the number of bins and let $\mathbf{p} = (p_1, \ldots, p_k)$ and
$\mathbf{q} = (q_1, \ldots, q_k)$ be two non-negative frequency vectors with
equal totals $\sum_i p_i = \sum_i q_i = n$. Define their cumulative sums:
$$
P(i) = \sum_{j=1}^{i} p_j, \qquad Q(i) = \sum_{j=1}^{i} q_j.
$$

The ground distance between bins is $d(i, j) = |i - j|$.

---

## The EMD as a transportation problem

The Earth Mover's Distance (Rubner et al. 2000) is

$$
\mathrm{EMD}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q})
  = \min_{\{t_{ij}\}} \sum_{i,j} t_{ij}\, |i - j|
$$

subject to

$$
\sum_j t_{ij} = p_i \;\; \forall i, \qquad
\sum_i t_{ij} = q_j \;\; \forall j, \qquad
t_{ij} \geq 0.
$$

The $t_{ij}$ represent how much mass is transported from bin $i$ to bin $j$.

---

## Main result

**Theorem.**
$$
\mathrm{EMD}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} |P(i) - Q(i)|.
$$

Because $P(k) = Q(k) = n$, the $i = k$ term vanishes and the sum effectively
runs over the $k - 1$ gaps between adjacent bins.

---

## Proof

### Lower bound

The integer $|i - j|$ counts the number of adjacent gaps crossed when moving
one unit of mass from bin $i$ to bin $j$:
$$
|i - j| = \#\{\ell : \min(i,j) \leq \ell < \max(i,j)\}.
$$

Substituting and exchanging the order of summation:
$$
\sum_{i,j} t_{ij}\, |i - j|
  = \sum_{\ell=1}^{k-1}
    \underbrace{\left(
      \sum_{\substack{i \leq \ell \\ j > \ell}} t_{ij}
      +
      \sum_{\substack{i > \ell \\ j \leq \ell}} t_{ij}
    \right)}_{\text{total flow crossing gap } \ell}.
$$

Let $R_\ell$ and $L_\ell$ denote the rightward and leftward flow across gap
$\ell$, respectively. Their difference is fixed by the marginal constraints:
the mass in $\mathbf{p}$ at positions $\leq \ell$ is $P(\ell)$, and after
transport it must equal $Q(\ell)$, so
$$
R_\ell - L_\ell = P(\ell) - Q(\ell).
$$

Since total flow at each gap is at least the absolute net flow,
$$
R_\ell + L_\ell \geq |R_\ell - L_\ell| = |P(\ell) - Q(\ell)|.
$$

Summing over all gaps:
$$
\sum_{i,j} t_{ij}\, |i - j|
  = \sum_{\ell=1}^{k-1} (R_\ell + L_\ell)
  \geq \sum_{\ell=1}^{k-1} |P(\ell) - Q(\ell)|.
$$

This holds for every feasible plan, so
$\mathrm{EMD}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) \geq \sum_\ell |P(\ell) - Q(\ell)|$.

### Achievability

It remains to exhibit a plan that attains this bound. A plan is tight if and
only if it has no countercurrents, i.e.\ $R_\ell \cdot L_\ell = 0$ for every
gap $\ell$. Such a plan exists: process bins left to right, carrying a running
surplus $\beta \geq 0$ from left to right.

Initialize $\beta = 0$. At each bin $i$, add the local surplus $p_i - q_i$ to
$\beta$. When $\beta > 0$, surplus mass from the left is waiting to fill
deficit bins further right; when $\beta < 0$, deficit mass is waiting for
supply from the right. The net rightward flow across gap $\ell$ is $\beta$
after processing bin $\ell$, which equals $P(\ell) - Q(\ell)$.

At every gap this plan flows purely rightward (when $P(\ell) > Q(\ell)$) or
purely leftward (when $P(\ell) < Q(\ell)$), so $R_\ell + L_\ell = |P(\ell) -
Q(\ell)|$ with no countercurrent. The total cost is
$\sum_{\ell=1}^{k-1} |P(\ell) - Q(\ell)|$, matching the lower bound.

### Conclusion

Combining both parts:
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{EMD}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} |P(i) - Q(i)|.}
$$

$\blacksquare$

---

## Relationship to Ling & Okada (2006)

Ling & Okada prove a more general version for 2D histograms, showing that the
full LP for EMD simplifies under the L₁ Manhattan ground distance (their
Proposition, Section 3.2). In 2D, eliminating long-range flows in favour of
neighbor flows reduces the LP variables from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N)$, yielding
their Tree-EMD algorithm with $O(N^2)$ empirical complexity.

The 1D case is a special instance where the simplification is complete: the LP
collapses to a closed form. The cut argument above shows that no optimization
is needed at all — the minimum is uniquely determined by the running CDF
differences, giving an $O(k)$ algorithm.

This equivalence is also noted by Levina & Bickel (2001), who show that the
EMD equals the Wasserstein-1 distance for 1D distributions, which in turn
equals the $L_1$ distance between CDFs.

---

## Note on normalization

The result above applies to unnormalized vectors (both summing to $n$). The
normalized version, with both vectors summing to 1, gives an EMD that is $1/n$
times the unnormalized one. For the purpose of ranking samples by distance to a
group centroid — as in medoid selection — the factor of $n$ is constant across
all comparisons and cancels.

---
